title: A Treasure Map Points to Earth's Missing Fossils
summary:
Fossils are our window into Earth's distant past, showing the animals, plants, and ecosystems that lived millions of years ago. But it tells only part of the story. Turning into a fossil is exceptionally rare, so only a tiny fraction of the creatures that once lived have been preserved. Even then, scientists can only find them where the rock layers are open to view.

That leaves big gaps in our picture of prehistoric life. Some periods and places have produced plenty of fossils; others remain largely unexplored. Digging takes a lot of time and money, so knowing where to look could make a major difference.

Two paleontologists have built a tool to help. Thomas A. Neubauer of the Bavarian State Collections of Natural History and Mathias Harzhauser of the Natural History Museum in Vienna studied fossils of animals that lived in shallow seas over the past 540 million years. For the first time, they also mapped the places where fossil information is missing.

They worked from the Paleobiology Database, the world's leading free collection of fossil records, plus geological information. That showed where fossils have already been found, and where the right kinds of rock could fill gaps.

The results held a surprise. The oldest periods, the Palaeozoic and the Early Mesozoic, have already been studied so much that new finds there are unlikely to add much knowledge soon. The best chances lie in more recent history: the Cenozoic Era, which began 66 million years ago. Its shallow sea deposits still hold great untapped potential.

The researchers pinpointed spots where unknown fossil species are especially likely to be found, and where the rock layers are exposed and reachable. Their map could help scientists plan better digs and spend limited research money wisely, focusing on "these still largely unexplored areas."
why_it_matters: Fossils are our best clues about how life on Earth changed over millions of years. A map of where to dig means scientists can find more of those clues without wasting time and money.
